planets.summary: "Disagrees sometimes" reads as a quirk; "serves your success, not your comfort" reads as a contract — a design constraint you can hold a transcript accountable to.
planets.content:
# The Advisor as Servant-Leader

> "Disagrees sometimes" reads as a quirk; "serves your success, not your comfort" reads as a
> contract — a design constraint you can hold a transcript accountable to.

## The connection
Servant-leadership inverts the usual power posture: the leader serves the led, and the highest
service is candor — telling the hard truth the person needs, not the flattery they want. That is
precisely the voice you want from an AI advisor: candid, willing to disagree, optimizing for the
user's outcome rather than their momentary comfort. The two are the same stance in two vocabularies
— one from leadership ethics, one from product UX.

Naming it as servant-leadership gives the advisor's tone a *principle* instead of a personality
quirk. "Disagrees sometimes" reads as a quirk; "serves your success, not your comfort" reads as a
contract. The first is a style knob; the second is a design constraint you can hold a transcript
accountable to.

## Why it matters
For any advisory product, voice is the trust surface. A flatterer feels good and converts worse on
the thing that matters — the user leaving with a clearer, truer picture. Framing the system prompt
and tone explicitly around servant-leadership ("in service of the user's success, even when that
means disagreeing") gives a testable rubric: does the advisor surface the inconvenient truth, or
smooth it over?

## So what
- Encode the posture in the advisor's system prompt as an explicit principle, not just "be candid."
- Add a transcript review rubric: did it tell a hard truth the user needed? Did it decline to
  flatter?
- Watch the failure mode — servant ≠ harsh. Service includes warmth; candor without care is just
  rudeness.

planets.title: The AI-Augmented Second Brain Stack
planets.summary: A second brain has three layers: a markdown-and-graph memory, AI agents as workers, and a loop where the system improves itself. The differentiator isn't the model — it's edge quality.
planets.content:
# The AI-Augmented Second Brain Stack

> A second brain has three layers: a markdown-and-graph memory, AI agents as workers, and a loop
> where the system improves itself. The differentiator isn't the model — it's edge quality.

## The connection
A cluster of ideas about running an AI-powered knowledge system all point at the same setup: a
local, plain-text vault as the memory, AI agents as the workers, and a loop where the system
improves itself. Stitched together, they form one blueprint.

## The stack
- **Memory layer.** Markdown notes + a link graph. Plain text you own, that any tool can read, with
  the graph as the structure.
- **Worker layer.** Coding agents and sub-agents that read, write, ingest, and synthesize against
  the vault — the "AI worker that runs while you sleep" pattern.
- **Shared-context layer.** A shared brain across agents so multiple workers operate on the same
  memory without drifting, plus reusable skills/plugins that encode repeatable workflows.
- **Self-improvement loop.** The vault generates its own candidate connections for a human to
  review — exploration writes edges, review keeps them honest.

## Why it matters
The point isn't reading *about* this stack — it's operating it. The defensible asset isn't the model
(anyone can call one); it's the curated, linked memory and the loop that keeps enriching it. The
stack is portable across any domain you work in.

## So what
- Keep the memory in plain text + links so it outlives any single tool.
- Formalize the repeatable workflows (ingest, synthesize, publish) as skills/commands rather than
  one-off prompts.
- Treat the self-improvement loop as the engine: it's what turns a notebook into a brain.

planets.title: The Barrier Is the Notation (Symbol Terror Is an Onboarding Tax)
planets.summary: The blocker is never the idea, it's the **notation**. Good teaching pays the toll for the learner: translate the symbols first, then the idea arrives free.
planets.content:
# The Barrier Is the Notation (Symbol Terror Is an Onboarding Tax)

> The blocker is never the idea, it's the **notation**. Good teaching pays the toll for the
> learner: translate the symbols first, then the idea arrives free.

## The connection
*Calculus Made Easy* (1910) and a "for people intimidated by the math" cheat sheet sell the
identical move: the blocker is never the idea, it's the **notation**. Thompson's whole first
chapter just renames symbols in plain English — `d` = "a little bit of," `∫` = "the sum of" — and
the fundamental theorem becomes obvious. Both reveal that unexplained primitives raise the
*activation energy* before any concept can land. The concept was always within reach; the glyphs
were a tollbooth. Good teaching pays the toll for the learner: translate symbols first, then the
idea arrives free.

## Why it matters
This generalizes far past math, straight into **product and onboarding**. Every tool has a
"notation": jargon, dense UI, unexplained primitives, an empty-state that assumes fluency. That
notation is the real adoption barrier — the activation energy a new user pays before they get any
value. Domains thick with codes, acronyms, and insider terms are especially exposed. The winning
onboarding move is Thompson's: say what each primitive *means* in plain English at the moment it
first appears, instead of assuming fluency.

## So what
- Audit onboarding for "symbol terror": every code, term, or primitive a first-time user meets gets
  a one-line plain-English gloss inline.
- Treat first-value time as activation energy to *minimize* — translate before you ask the user to
  act.
- Reuse the "rename the symbol" trick in your own learning: when stuck, suspect the notation, not
  the concept.

planets.title: The Brain Is a Self-Improving Harness (Sparks Explore, Neurons Consolidate)
planets.summary: A second brain isn't a notebook, or even a graph — it's a *harness that improves its own scaffolding*: explore cheaply, consolidate the best, and keep a human gate as the regularizer.
planets.content:
# The Brain Is a Self-Improving Harness (Sparks Explore, Neurons Consolidate)

> A second brain isn't a notebook, or even a graph — it's a *harness that improves its own
> scaffolding*: explore cheaply, consolidate the best, and keep a human gate as the regularizer.

## The connection
A **harness** is the scaffolding around a language model (tools, prompts, control flow, retry and
memory loop) that turns a raw model into an agent — and a **self-harness** is one that **optimizes
its own scaffolding** instead of being hand-tuned. The minimal version is a **plan → execute →
read-own-output → fix** loop that runs until success.

That is a precise description of a self-synthesizing knowledge base. The pieces map one-to-one:

| Self-improving harness | The synthesis loop |
|---|---|
| Exploration / sampling | **Sparks** — cheap, 2-line candidate connections, cast widely |
| Consolidation / policy update | **Neurons** — promote the best spark into a full framework note |
| Reward signal | **Triage** — promote good sparks, delete dead ones |
| Training loop / scheduler | A periodic synthesis run |
| Learned representation | The **graph** — every neuron adds edges; retrieval gets faster |
| Scaffolding being optimized | The capture → ingest → map → synthesize workflow itself |

## Why it matters
It names what a vault is becoming: not a notebook, not even a graph, but a *harness that improves its
own scaffolding*. The actionable gap is closing the loop: today the human is the reward function
(promote/delete). The frontier move is an agentic synthesis pass that proposes *and pre-scores*
candidate connections against the existing graph (novelty, support, cross-domain distance), so you
only adjudicate the top few.

The built-in caution: an unsupervised pattern-finder will **overfit** — it mints spurious
connections (apophenia). The cure is out-of-sample validation. So the human triage isn't a
bottleneck to automate away — it's the **regularizer / holdout** that keeps the harness honest.
Automate the *proposing and scoring*; keep a human *gate* on promotion.

## So what
- Treat the synthesis loop as a product with a roadmap, not a cron job: instrument it (sparks
  promoted vs deleted = the harness's hit-rate), and add an automated pre-score step before the
  human gate.
- Keep the human gate as the regularizer — automate proposal and scoring, never the final promote
  decision.

- Treat skipped constraints as the accident chain, not as a flex.

Felids keep a core they will fight for and a buffer they will share. The peace is the buffer, not the friendship. Walk into the core uninvited and you get a stare. Knowledge graphs fail when they treat every overlap as a core to capture. Two notes can share a buffer without surrendering a range. The constellation should get planets that claimed a patch and left a hallway, not planets that sat on another star's sill and called it hygiene. A buffer you can refuse is a slow blink. A core you cannot leave is a stare.

## So what
- Keep a buffer between cores. A spark is a hallway. A forced merge is a stare into the nest.
- When two notes scrape fur, widen the buffer. Do not annex the core and call it cleanup.
- Publish into a patch you can hold. Leave the neighboring core alone until there is a treaty.

planets.content:
# The Fan-Out Port (Design as Spec, Parallel Porters, Build-Verify)

> The quality comes from the **contract + the verify**, not from each agent being perfect. It turns
> "weeks of mechanical work" into one wall-clock pass.

## The connection
Large mechanical jobs — porting a design to code, ingesting hundreds of documents, auditing a big
corpus — all go the same way when run with parallel agents. The shared shape is **the Fan-Out
Port**:
1. **Design/spec is the source of truth** — not memory.
2. **Decompose into independent units** with no overlap (one screen / one document-block / one
   range).
3. **Fan out parallel agents** against a **shared contract** — a low-error-surface convention that
   makes the common mistake impossible (e.g. a helper that prevents a class of formatting failure;
   disjoint number ranges so outputs can't collide).
4. **Central build-verify** — a deterministic gate (a build, a test suite) catches the integration
   errors no single agent can see.

It's the self-improving harness applied to *construction*: exploration = the parallel porters;
consolidation = the build-verify gate.

## Why it matters
The quality comes from the **contract + the verify**, not from each agent being perfect. The failure
modes are predictable: (a) no shared contract → inconsistent output; (b) overlapping units →
collisions; (c) no verify → silent breakage. This is the build-time twin of "10% model, 90%
plumbing."

## So what
- Make "Fan-Out Port" the default for any large transform: migration, port, ingest, audit,
  long-form generation.
- Always ship three things with the fan-out: a **convention** that removes the common error,
  **disjoint units**, and a **deterministic verify** plus a tiny **completeness scan** for
  cross-unit invariants (valid references, no dupes).

# The First Solo Evaporates the Instructor

> Dual time is the barrel with a teacher in the right seat. The first solo is the angel's share: a few percent of the system disappears on purpose, and what remains has to hold heading alone.

[[First Solo Is Attitude, Not Hours]] says the certificate is not the hours — it is one circuit without the instructor's hands. [[The Angel's Share Buys the Edge]] says the missing percent is the fee that makes the liquid pourable. The shared mechanism is proof-by-absence. If the airplane only flies because someone is on the stick, you do not have a pilot. If the note only stands because you are in the room to explain the names, you do not have a planet.

Barrel time without evaporation is a sealed cask. Dual time without a solo is a logbook. Both look like work. Neither is a heading another person can take. The constellation cannot see a student who never leaves the right seat, and it should not drink a spirit that never paid the share.

## Why it holds
- The proof is counterfactual. Remove the helper (instructor, private context, client name). If attitude holds, you have a planet.
- Volume loss is the point. Genericizing is evaporation, not theft from yourself.
- Currency is more circuits, not a bigger engine. One lucky solo is not an ATP. One lucky publish is not a cluster.

## So what (the actionable edge)
- Before you publish, evaporate the instructor: read the note as a stranger in the county. If it needs you, it is still dual.
- Solo a small pattern — a few linked planets — rather than logging another hundred private hours.

planets.title: The Graph Compounds Like Interest
planets.summary: A note that just sits there adds *principal*. A note that connects to many others earns on the *running total*. The value of a knowledge graph is the edge set, not the node count — and like compound interest, it goes slow-then-sudden.
planets.content:
# The Graph Compounds Like Interest

> A note that just sits there adds *principal*. A note that connects to many others earns on the
> *running total*. The value of a knowledge graph is the edge set, not the node count — and like
> compound interest, it goes slow-then-sudden.

## The connection
Simple interest grows on principal alone — `A = P(1 + r·t)`, linear. Compound interest grows on
the running total — `A = P(1 + r)^t`, exponential, because each period's gain earns the next. A
knowledge base compounds the same way. A new isolated note adds linear principal (one more node).
A new **synthesis note that links many prior notes** grows the accumulated connectivity — value
on the running total, not the principal.

## Why it matters
The defensible asset in a second brain is the **curated edge set**, not the raw note count.
Anyone can copy your pipeline in an afternoon; nobody can copy months of connections. The
reinvestment rate `r` is your **synthesis cadence**. Skipping a synthesis cycle isn't a flat
loss — it's forgone compounding that permanently lowers the curve.

## So what
- Treat the periodic synthesis pass as a non-skippable reinvestment payment.
- Measure the system by **edge growth / connectivity**, not note count.
- Prune aggressively — dead links and stale half-ideas are *negative* interest on the principal.

planets.title: The Holdout Rule (Graded Systems Need Out-of-Sample)
planets.summary: Anything that grades against a metric needs a holdout — an out-of-sample check the optimizer never saw. It's the difference between a score that *looks* rigorous and one that *is*.
planets.content:
# The Holdout Rule (Graded Systems Need Out-of-Sample)

> Anything that grades against a metric needs a holdout — an out-of-sample check the optimizer
> never saw. It's the difference between a score that *looks* rigorous and one that *is*.

## The connection
A quant strategy tuned until it aces its **backtest** and a document tuned until it aces a **scoring
rubric** suffer the identical failure: **optimizing the proxy until it stops predicting reality**
(overfitting / Goodhart's law — "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure").
Every graded product is exposed to this:
- An idea success-score could be gamed by phrasing ideas to score well without being better ideas.
- A compliance rubric could be satisfied by a packet tuned to pass while missing the real risk.
- A citation verifier could be satisfied by a document that's still misleading in aggregate.

## The rule
**Anything that grades against a metric needs a holdout — an out-of-sample check the optimizer never
saw.** In trading that's walk-forward / out-of-sample testing; in ML it's the test set; for any
graded product it means a second, independent signal the score can't be gamed against:
- Validate a sample of high-scoring outputs against *real outcomes*, not just re-scoring.
- Use an independent human review as the holdout the rubric is measured against — and periodically
  re-audit "passing" results for real deficiencies.
- Spot-check a random sample, and track real-world error escapes.

## So what
Add a "holdout / anti-gaming" section to any rubric spec: every graded product ships with (1) a
metric, and (2) an independent out-of-sample validation that catches when the metric is being gamed.

A mash bill is the recipe: corn, rye, malt, the ratios you can write on a card. The drink is the liquid after wood, weather, and evaporation have had a vote. Outline a note and you have mash. People confuse the recipe with the pour because the recipe is fast and the barrel is slow. A constellation that indexes mash bills will taste like a pitch deck. Time in the wood still matters. So does the neighborhood the cask sat in. The graph is the warehouse climate.

## So what
- Score a note by the graph it sits in, not by the outline it started as.
- Do not publish the mash bill and call it a tasting.
- If two notes share a recipe but not a warehouse, they are not the same drink.

Heroics on a bad glideslope are a brief you skipped, then tried to replace with throttle.

- Ego wants to stick the landing. The airplane wants a brief that still fits the slope.
- The public map should get planets that arrived with a card, not performances that arrived hot.

## So what (the actionable edge)
- Write the hold-private into the capture card before you try to publish.
- When the approach is unstable, fly the missed approach you already named. Do not invent heroics in the flare.

planets.title: The Missing Money Node (Idea→Revenue Audit)
planets.summary: A feature is only done when its conversion edge works end-to-end — no dead CTAs, no placeholder stubs, no gate that approves work but releases nothing. Every feature needs a working money node.
planets.content:
# The Missing Money Node (Idea→Revenue Audit)

> A feature is only done when its conversion edge works end-to-end — no dead CTAs, no placeholder
> stubs, no gate that approves work but releases nothing. Every feature needs a working money node.

## The pattern
The common failure: every stage of the funnel gets built except the one where money changes hands.
The product implements `Data → Work → Insight → Decisions` and stops one arrow short of
`→ Revenue`. The symptoms are recognizable:
- The top-of-funnel CTA is a stub — a button that pops an alert or a `mailto:` instead of capturing
  the lead and carrying it into the system built to receive it.
- Approval gates exist and are audited, but **nothing is bound to them** — the gate proves a
  milestone was accepted and then does nothing with the one thing acceptance was supposed to
  trigger (the release of funds, the invoice, the next tranche).
- The cheapest artifact has the most complete payment path while the flagship has none —
  monetization gravity inverted, the toy can take a dollar but the business cannot.

## Why it matters
A trust machine that grades and audits work is one step from completion: the gates *grade* the work,
so payment should be the **payout function of the grade**. If the revenue edge isn't wired, the
audit log is a seam waiting for the one edge that makes the whole promise real. Two structural
failures recur portfolio-wide: no first-dollar path wired into the flagship, and no venture with
time-bound kill criteria.

## So what
1. **Bind money to gates.** On gate-approved → generate the phase invoice / payment link for that
   tranche. The audit log is already the event seam.
2. **Revive dead CTAs.** Every conversion button posts a real lead into the system, with a real
   follow-up, using infrastructure that already exists.
3. **Put pricing inside the product.** Generate the price from the captured inputs; kill "as quoted
   separately."
4. **Keep a first-dollar scoreboard.** One visible number: $ collected, deals signed, leads captured
   this week. Goals can't be hit unmeasured.
5. **Run a kill-criteria pass.** Add time-bound, measurable kill criteria to each active project
   *before* calling anything "on track."

planets.content:
# The Rickhouse Is a Neighborhood

> Barrels age by shared climate, not in a closet. Notes age by sitting next to other notes. A lone cask is not a rickhouse.

A rickhouse is a neighborhood with weather. Barrels share heat, humidity, leaks in the roof. The same mash in two warehouses is two drinks because the neighbors were different. Aging a note in a private folder with no wiki-links is a cask in a closet. Time passed. Climate did not. People confuse duration with aging. A note that sat alone for a year is still n=1 with a birthday. The wood is the graph. Neighbors are the climate. Publishing a planet that never sat beside another planet is pouring closet whiskey and calling it a rickhouse. The public universe should taste warehouse weather, not a timer.

## So what
- Age a note next to two neighbors before you pour. Time without climate is a closet.
- Treat a wiki-link as shared weather, not as decoration on a solitary cask.
- If a claim never sat in a row, it is not aged. It is stored. Move it into the rickhouse.

planets.title: The Rubric Pattern (Graded, Explainable AI Is the Trust Primitive)
planets.summary: Intelligence is table stakes; trust is the product. The trust primitive is the rubric: a fixed, weighted, explainable scoring scheme graded against ground truth — never raw model output on faith.
planets.content:
# The Rubric Pattern (Graded, Explainable AI Is the Trust Primitive)

> Intelligence is table stakes; trust is the product. The trust primitive is the rubric: a fixed,
> weighted, explainable scoring scheme graded against ground truth — never raw model output on
> faith.

## The connection
The same design move recurs across otherwise-unrelated AI builds: **define a fixed, weighted,
explainable scoring or verification scheme and grade outputs against a ground truth — never trust
raw model output on faith.** A benchmark that scores generated work across weighted dimensions with
auto-fail triggers; a verifier that grades each claim against its primary source and blocks shipping
on failure; an idea-validator that ranks with a weighted success score *and explains why*; a
synthetic-data harness that grades decisions against known-correct ground truth — they all
independently converge on the same trust mechanism.

## Why it matters
The real product DNA isn't "AI that's smart" — it's "AI whose output is graded, explainable, and
trustworthy." Every flagship artifact converging on the same trust mechanism isn't coincidence;
it's the instinct worth naming. "Graded, auditable AI" is a sharper pitch than "AI-powered," and
it's exactly what high-stakes buyers want: operational reliability over raw cleverness. It's also
harder to copy — anyone can call a model; a transparent grading layer that buyers can audit is the
defensible part.

## So what
- Extract a shared **rubric engine**: define dimensions + weights + ground-truth source + pass/fail
  gates, and reuse it across products. One core, many applications.
- Lead with it: pitch "graded, auditable AI," not "AI-powered."
- Treat the grading layer as the trust surface — make it transparent enough that a skeptical buyer
  can audit the score.

planets.title: The Slow Blink Is a Cheap Consent Signal
planets.summary: A cat's hard stare is a threat display. The slow blink is the opposite protocol: I see you, I am not hunting, you may come closer. It is cheap, bidirectional, and easy to refuse.
planets.content:
# The Slow Blink Is a Cheap Consent Signal

> A cat's hard stare is a threat display. The slow blink is the opposite protocol: I see you, I am not hunting, you may come closer. It is cheap, bidirectional, and easy to refuse.

## The connection
Consent in a constellation is supposed to look like a signed publish. The everyday version is smaller. A spark, a wiki-link, a note held private on purpose — those are slow blinks. Dumping a whole vault into the universe is a stare. Grooming in a macaque troop is costly and public; a cat blink is almost free. You need both. The costly gate (barrel, license, signature) keeps the pour honest. The cheap blink is how two animals agree to close the distance at all.

## Why it matters
Trust systems that only have stares — mandatory reviews, all-to-all sharing, "just make it public" — produce freezing, not approach. Isolates often stare because they never learned the cheap first edge. A White Out works because you can stay home. A blink that cannot be refused is a stare wearing a smile.

## So what
- Offer edges that can be ignored. A spark is a blink. A forced link is a stare.
- Read silence as a refused blink, not as a bug in the other star.
- First contact should be one planet, not a stare into their whole graph.

planets.title: A Linked Vault Wants to Be a Graph RAG
planets.summary: A linked note vault is already a hand-built knowledge graph. Most graph-RAG systems build the graph *graph-last* by extraction; a curated vault was built *graph-first* by hand — and that inversion is the advantage.
planets.content:
# A Linked Vault Wants to Be a Graph RAG

> A linked note vault is already a hand-built knowledge graph. Most graph-RAG systems build the
> graph *graph-last* by extraction; a curated vault was built *graph-first* by hand — and that
> inversion is the advantage.

## The connection
A linked note vault is a **knowledge graph**: nodes (notes) + typed edges (wiki-links), with hub
notes, origin-colored authorship, and synthesis notes bridging clusters. That's not a metaphor —
it's literally the substrate every "Graph RAG" system tries to construct from scratch. The road from
*static graph* to *queryable second brain* runs through two architectures: **Graph RAG** (retrieve
over entity/relationship structure, not flat text) and **Agentic RAG** (an agent with memory +
planning orchestrates multi-step retrieval). The vault's links *are* the graph edges Graph RAG
needs; the hub notes are pre-built entry nodes.

## Why it matters
The vault was built **graph-first by hand** (you wrote the edges); RAG systems are usually built
**graph-last by extraction** (an LLM guesses the edges from a text dump). That inversion is an
advantage: retrieval quality is bounded by edge quality, and curated, origin-tagged, deliberately
bridged edges are far richer than auto-extracted ones. So the missing piece isn't structure, it's
the **retrieval + agent layer**: a vector index for semantic recall, graph traversal that follows
links and hub membership (not just cosine similarity), and an agent loop with memory that plans
multi-hop queries across clusters.

## So what
- Point a Graph-RAG retriever at the vault: semantic search to find seed notes, then traverse links
  + shared hubs one or two hops to assemble context, then answer.
- Treat synthesis notes as high-value "bridge" context — they connect clusters, so they pull the
  most cross-domain signal into an answer.
- It compounds the existing loop: the synthesis pass *writes* edges; a retrieval layer *reads* them.
  Together that's a brain that both forms and recalls connections.

planets.title: Throughput Comes From Removing Contention, Not From Tidiness
planets.summary: A "tidy"-looking ordering optimizes for legibility, not throughput. Throughput is set by the *contended resource*.
planets.content:
# Throughput Comes From Removing Contention, Not From Tidiness

> A "tidy"-looking ordering optimizes for legibility, not throughput. Throughput is set by the
> *contended resource*.

## The connection
Back-to-front airplane boarding is the slowest method for the exact reason naive multithreading is
slow: everyone contends for one shared resource (the aisle and overhead bin) at the same time, so
the work *serializes* even though many people could be acting at once. That's concurrency without
parallelism — lots of "active" agents, one core. The fast boarding methods are **lock-free
parallelism**: order passengers so adjacent ones never touch the same resource simultaneously,
maximizing how many bags get stowed in parallel. The deep point: a tidy-looking ordering (strict
back-to-front) optimizes for legibility, not throughput. Throughput is set by the *contended
resource* — keep it busy with non-conflicting work and you go fast; pile everyone onto it at once
and ordering barely matters.

## Why it matters
This is one rule spanning cabins, cores, pipelines, and teams — practical anywhere a queue feels
slow despite "being organized."

## So what
- To speed any pipeline, don't sort it neatly — **identify the contended resource and schedule to
  keep it busy with non-conflicting work**. Tidiness is a red herring; contention is the
  constraint.
- Software: prefer lock-free / sharded designs where threads touch disjoint data over a single big
  lock everyone queues on. CI: parallelize jobs that don't share a runner/artifact rather than
  ordering them prettily.
- Teams and ops: batch and interleave work so people aren't all blocked on the same shared step
  (one reviewer, one system, one inbox). Find the single shared step and either shard it or stagger
  arrivals — controlled interleaving beats orderly queuing.

# Titles Chase the Current Graph

## The connection
[[Rank Is a Lagging Indicator]] says the org chart is last week's grooming graph. Trust routes along current edges: who grooms whom this morning, not who held the top perch last season. A title is a photograph printed after the sitting. [[Social Grooming Is the Real API]] says the real routing table is who spends costly time on whom. - The print is always late. Rank is a photograph. Grooming is the weather.
- Load routes along current edges, not along last season's perch.
- A folder that disagrees with a wiki-link is an org chart arguing with this morning's sitting.

## So what (the actionable edge)
- Trust the live edges over the printed rank.
- When a folder and a wiki-link disagree, believe the link.
- Treat a new title as a lagging report, not as a routing change. Do not wait for the reprint to sit.

# Trim Tabs Beat Thrust

> A jet can have all the thrust in the world and still fly crooked. The little tab on the elevator is what lets the airplane hold attitude without the pilot leaning on the stick for the whole flight.

Thrust gets you off the ground. Trim is what makes the flight sustainable. The same split shows up in a second brain: capture is thrust (more notes, more topics, more heat). Publish-and-link is trim — a tiny signed correction that lets the graph hold heading. Buckminster Fuller used the trim tab as a civics metaphor for the same reason: the smallest surface, placed at the hinge, turns the largest mass.

Joining a public constellation by dumping a whole vault is more throttle. Joining with three opt-in planets — monkeys, whiskey, airplanes — is a trim tab. The universe does not need your entire brain. It needs a small, flyable attitude you can hold.

## So what
- Prefer one well-trimmed planet per topic over a cargo hold of unpublished heat.
- When the graph yaws (topics that do not connect), add a trim edge, not another engine.
- Fly the public map like a traffic pattern: opt in, show the diff, land, then go around if you need to unpublish.

planets.title: Trojan-Horse GTM (The Free Wedge Sells the Case Study)
planets.summary: A deliberately-free pilot isn't a discount — it's a distribution buy. Its real deliverable isn't the work performed; it's the measured, quotable proof that unlocks the channel that scales.
planets.content:
# Trojan-Horse GTM (The Free Wedge Sells the Case Study)

> A deliberately-free pilot isn't a discount — it's a distribution buy. Its real deliverable isn't
> the work performed; it's the measured, quotable proof that unlocks the channel that scales.

## The connection
A free or below-cost pilot looks like a services engagement, but its real deliverable isn't the work
performed — it's the **measured case study**. The pilot is a *distribution buy* disguised as a
giveaway: deliberately unprofitable, because the thing it purchases is proof, and the proof unlocks
the actual prize (a corporate channel, a marquee logo, an enterprise license whose economics dwarf
the wedge). This is land-and-expand where the land is intentionally free, because the expand is the
real business.

The Trojan-horse structure has a precondition that's easy to miss: the gift only converts if its
results are **instrumented to be quotable**. A free pilot that does the work but produces no clean,
attributable, before/after numbers buys nothing. So the wedge's success criterion is not "did it
work" but "can we *prove* it worked, in a sentence a buyer will repeat." That ties straight to the
rule that every gate must emit an event: the pilot's value is only realized if its outcomes are
captured as measured, citable events.

## Why it matters
A free or below-cost pilot isn't a discount — it's a marketing line item whose ROI is measured in
the channel it opens, not the revenue it books. The hard part of these businesses isn't the service;
it's manufacturing undeniable, transferable proof and routing it into the channel that scales.

## So what
- Score every "free pilot" by the prize it's buying (channel access, marquee logo, case study), not
  by its own P&L.
- Instrument the wedge from day one: define the 2–3 metrics the case study must show, and wire the
  events that capture them before the pilot starts.
- Only run the deliberately-free wedge when the expand path is real and large enough to justify the
  loss-leader.

planets.summary: Don't average your virality drivers — one fatal zero shouldn't hide behind four strong scores. And the content is only the 10%; distribution is the 90%.
planets.content:
# Virality, Distribution & the Rubric

> Don't average your virality drivers — one fatal zero shouldn't hide behind four strong scores.
> And the content is only the 10%; distribution is the 90%.

## The pattern
A common model scores "will this spread?" by averaging a handful of drivers — emotion, identity,
timing, clarity, looping. Four failure modes recur in that kind of model:

1. **The equation shouldn't be an average.** A mean implies the drivers are *substitutable* — but
   emotional-but-confusing content fails. An average lets one fatal zero hide behind four strong
   scores. Fix: **weight** the load-bearing drivers higher, make it **multiplicative** so a
   near-zero on any driver tanks the whole score (a limiting-factor model), or treat **clarity as a
   gate** (pass/fail), not an additive term.
2. **The scores are post-hoc and circular.** Scoring cases *after* they're known to be viral is
   survivorship + hindsight bias. Validate by scoring *before* outcomes, and include false positives
   (high-scoring flops) and false negatives (low-scoring hits).
3. **The model ignores distribution — the bigger half.** Quality is necessary but not sufficient;
   seeding, network position, algorithm fit, and timing-luck decide reach. The post is the 10%,
   distribution is the 90%. Split the score into **Content Score × Distribution Score**.
4. **The scale needs anchors.** 1–5 is subjective; add a one-line behavioral anchor per score so
   it's a real rubric — graded, explainable — not a vibe.

## Why it matters
A virality scorecard is itself an instance of the rubric pattern: define weighted dimensions, score
against them, explain the score. Tightening it (multiplicative + anchored + a distribution factor)
turns it from a hindsight label into a predictive tool.

## So what
- The most viral asset usually isn't copy — it's a **shareable result artifact** (an output the
  user *wants* to post). Design the output to score high on the drivers itself.
- Ship the model as `min/weighted(drivers) × distribution`, with anchored 1–5 rubrics — then it's
  defensible and reusable.

planets.title: Volatility Harvesting (Feedback Control You Want Disturbed)
planets.summary: Turn the disturbance you'd normally fight into the thing you harvest. It's a design pattern, not just a trade.
planets.content:
# Volatility Harvesting (Feedback Control You Want Disturbed)

> Turn the disturbance you'd normally fight into the thing you harvest. It's a design pattern, not
> just a trade.

## The connection
Gamma scalping is textbook negative feedback. The trader holds long gamma, measures an error term
(net delta away from zero), and applies a proportional correction — sell underlying when price
rises, buy when it falls — driving delta back to a setpoint of zero. That's the same controller as
the inverted pendulum, the stop-loss, and the AI agent loop.

But it inverts the usual moral. Everywhere else, the disturbance is the enemy: you correct *against*
it and wish it would go away. In gamma scalping you **want the disturbance** — the underlying's
volatility is exactly what you're paid for. Each re-hedge locks in $\tfrac12\Gamma(dS)^2$; the
position is profitable whenever realized variance beats the theta you pay:
$\tfrac12\Gamma(dS)^2 > \Theta\,dt \Leftrightarrow \sigma_{\text{realized}} > \sigma_{\text{implied}}$.
So this is a controller that monetizes the very error it suppresses. The "cost of control" (theta)
is the premium, and the path variance you fight is the revenue.

## Why it matters
The general move — *turn the disturbance you'd normally fight into the thing you harvest* — is a
design pattern, not just a trade. Any self-correcting system that pays per correction (rebalancing,
market-making, even churn-driven re-engagement) is a volatility harvester. The question shifts from
"how do I eliminate variance?" to "is my correction cost lower than the variance I capture?"

## So what
- Frame any hedged position as a controller and ask the one question that decides P&L: realized vs.
  implied — is the gain (re-hedge frequency) tuned to capture variance without bleeding theta?
- Add a "disturbance polarity" axis when applying feedback control: for each system, is the
  disturbance a cost to suppress or a revenue to harvest? It changes whether you minimize or
  maximize loop gain.

planets.content:
# White-Out Is a Stadium-Scale Trim Tab

> A jet holds attitude with a tab you could hide in your palm. Beaver Stadium holds a single visible body with a rule you could hide in a text: wear white. Same physics. Different vehicle.

## The connection
[[Trim Tabs Beat Thrust]] is Fuller's civics metaphor wearing a flight-control surface: the smallest hinge turns the largest mass. [[White-Out Is One Constraint]] is the same hinge at 110,000 seats. You do not brief every section on heading. You pick one cheap, binary, public surface and let the crowd become the elevator.

Thrust in a stadium is more noise, more shirts, more brands on the jumbotron. That is how a regular Saturday looks from the press box — loud and unreadable as one organism. The White Out subtracts wardrobe (angel's share of color) and the camera finally gets a field. Publishing a star cluster works the same way. One license, one handle, a galaxy you can defend, titles that travel. That is trim. Dumping the vault is throttle.

Cats already know a cheaper version of the same signal: the slow blink is a one-bit constraint (not hunting) that lets two animals close distance. White Out is the blink at stadium gain. You can refuse it. That refusal is what makes the people who opt in a heading, not a coerced mass.

## Why it holds
- The control surface is small on purpose. Extra rules (second dress code, private jokes, a new ontology per note) split the stand the way a second tab fights the first.
- Opt-in is load-bearing. A forced White Out is a stare. A forced publish is thrust.
- Readability from orbit is the success metric. If another star cannot see the body, you are still a crowd.

## So what (the actionable edge)
- When the public map yaws, add one constraint, not another engine.
- Keep campus clothes in the vault. Wear the one publishable color on the field.
- If a new topic cannot keep the same dress code (genericized, signed, one galaxy), it is not ready for the stand.

## Sources

- [[Trim Tabs Beat Thrust]]
- [[The Slow Blink Is a Cheap Consent Signal]]

planets.title: Wiki-Links Are DNS for the Vault
planets.summary: If retrieval walks edges that don't resolve, the graph it traverses is a lie, and the answer inherits the lie.
planets.content:
# Wiki-Links Are DNS for the Vault

> If retrieval walks edges that don't resolve, the graph it traverses is a lie, and the answer
> inherits the lie.

## The connection
A `[[wiki-link]]` is a name→note resolution, exactly like a DNS A-record is name→IP. The whole DNS
record set maps onto vault link mechanics: an **A-record** is a link to a real note; a **CNAME** is
an alias (one name resolving to a canonical note); a broken link is a dangling **NXDOMAIN**; an
orphan note is an island no record points to. DNS doesn't trust the network until resolution is
healthy — and neither should a graph-based retrieval system. If retrieval walks edges that don't
resolve (or resolve ambiguously via stale aliases), the graph it traverses is a lie, and the answer
inherits the lie.

## Why it matters
This gives a graph-retrieval build a missing pre-index stage. It's tempting to assume links resolve;
DNS literacy says assume they don't until audited. A retrieval layer that trusts broken edges is the
streetlight failure in a new costume — confidently walking to a node that isn't there. The resolver
(link-integrity + alias table) is cheap, runs once per index, and gates trust.

## So what
- Add a link-resolution health check as a pre-index step: report broken links (NXDOMAIN), orphans,
  and duplicate/ambiguous aliases (CNAME collisions).
- Maintain an explicit alias table so retrieval resolves canonical names deterministically, not by
  fuzzy match.
- Fail the index (or flag) if broken-link count exceeds a threshold — don't ship retrieval over an
  unresolved graph.

planets.summary: You name the missed-approach field before you leave. A vault should name the hold-private before it tries to publish. Alternates are the card, not pessimism.
planets.content:
# You Brief the Alternate Before Takeoff

> You name the missed-approach field before you leave. A vault should name the hold-private before it tries to publish. Alternates are the card, not pessimism.

## The connection
A crew does not invent the alternate on short final. They brief it on the ground: fuel, weather, the field they will use if this runway is not theirs. The alternate is part of the takeoff brief, not a confession of failure. A vault that only plans the publish has no missed-approach field. Hold-private is the alternate. A go-around is flying it. Hero stories skip the field and then invent a recovery in the flare. That is how you bend metal.

## Why it matters
Competence hides the hole. You skip the alternate because the destination already feels like home. Vaults skip the hold-private because the note already feels done. The constellation should see planets that arrived with a field named, not performances that arrived with no fuel for a second try. Naming the alternate is trim. Inventing it on short final is thrust used as a substitute for a card.

## So what
- Name the hold-private before you try to publish. The alternate is part of the brief.
- Treat a go-around as flying the field you already named, not as a surprise failure.
- If you cannot name an alternate, you are not cleared. Stay on the ground until the card has a second field.

## Related

- [[A Go-Around Is a Success]]
- [[Trim Tabs Beat Thrust]]

planets.content:
# You Cannot Trim Unaged Distillate

> A trim tab works on an airplane that already flies. It does not turn raw mash into a heading. Unaged distillate has no attitude to hold. It has heat.

## The connection
[[Proof Needs Time in the Barrel]] is a control loop with a long sample interval. Distillation is high-gain and noisy. The barrel is the filter. [[Trim Tabs Beat Thrust]] says the little surface on the elevator is what lets you hold attitude without leaning on the stick. Thrust gets you off the ground. Trim makes the flight sustainable.

The spark's claim is the order of operations. You cannot trim a spirit that never sat in wood. Publish-and-link is trim applied to aged distillate, not more throttle on the still. Dumping the inbox into the constellation is thrust on hot product. A tiny signed planet, genericized and linked, is trim on something that already had years.

Fuller used the tab as civics because the smallest hinge turns the largest mass. The mass has to exist first. A vault that only captures is a still with no rickhouse. A vault that only publishes is a tab bolted to vapor.

## Why it holds
- Sequence is load-bearing. Barrel then trim. Distill then age then a small surface.
- Heat is not attitude. High-proof first pours yaw under any tab.
- The public map should get flyable planets, not more engine on unaged mash.

## So what (the actionable edge)
- Age the note against two neighbors before you add the trim edge.
- When the graph yaws, do not open the still. Ask what the barrel subtracted, then tap the tab.
- If a claim is still hot distillate, hold-private. Trim is not a substitute for wood.
